title: Case study: tourism at Etosha National Park, Namibia

blocks.heading: The case study: an area where tourism is important
blocks.text: Etosha National Park in Namibia - what attracts its visitors, why tourism matters to the people around it, and how the park is managed so the visits can continue.

blocks.heading: Etosha National Park
blocks.text: Etosha National Park covers about 22 000 square kilometres of dry woodland and grassland in northern Namibia, around a salt pan so large it dominates the park's centre. Visitors stay at the state rest camps at Okaukuejo, Halali and Namutoni, each built beside an artificial waterhole. The waterholes are the great attraction: elephants, giraffes, zebras, lions and the black rhinos Etosha is known for protecting come to drink, and at Okaukuejo the waterhole is lit at night so visitors can watch after dark. The park received roughly 200 000 visitors a year in the late 2010s (rounded figure), arriving by road from Windhoek or through Outjo.

blocks.heading: Why tourism matters around Etosha
blocks.text: The region is dry, with unreliable rainfall and little other employment, so the park's conservation fees and rest-camp wages are a foundation of the local economy. Because the wildlife stays protected, the earnings continue: visitors pay precisely because the animals are there. Outside the gates, neighbouring communal conservancies - registered areas where a community holds the rights to manage and benefit from its wildlife - receive levies from joint-venture lodges, so tourism income reaches villages that never see a tourist bus. The same fees fund anti-poaching patrols and wildlife monitoring, which keep the attraction alive.

blocks.heading: The management, and why it works
blocks.text: The management follows the place's limits. Beds are capped at the three state rest camps instead of allowing hotels to spread across the park; day visitors pay a conservation fee on entry; speed limits and a ban on off-road driving protect the animals and the pan's fragile crust. The result is a park where the visits that pay for conservation are kept small enough not to damage what they pay for - management as the condition of the income, not its enemy.
